utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr., Bourgon; Mr. Petrusic - here or not? yeah - and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey present, accompanied by Mr. Thayer. I understand there are no preliminaries. The witness is also present. Good morning, to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing by the truth. You have been summoned here as a witness by the Defence team for Ljubisa Beara. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Who is going to -- Mr. Nikolic from the Beara Defence team will be examining you in chief, and he will then be followed on cross-examination by others. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We have already met, but just for the record I would like to give you some instructions to facilitate our work. This primarily concerns our communication. We both speak the Serbian language, which needs to be translated. That's why I'm going to ask you to make a short pause after my question before starting your answer, and this will be of some benefit to everybody in the courtroom. Let me first introduce myself: Predrag Nikolic, co-counsel on the Beara Defence team. And can I now please ask you to introduce yourself; give us your first name, last name, the date and place of birth and all the particulars that are necessary for your identification.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Vojinovic, born in 1959 in Sarajevo. I reside in Sokolac, 40 kilometres away from Sarajevo, in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I finished the secondary school for the interior in Sarajevo in 1977. Between 1980 and 1983, I attended the school of security in Skoplje and I attained a agree in security law, associate degree in security law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us something about your professional background, first before the war and then during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war broke out in 1992, which means from 1977 to 1992, I worked in the Ministry of the Interior of the then Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the Public Security Service which during that period of time existed in Sokolac, and that's where I worked in the police station, or as we call it, the station for the police. I performed and discharged various duties starting with policeman, the head of patrol, inspector in crime prevention police for general crime, and then I worked in the traffic control, and for awhile I also discharged the duties of the assistant head of the police station, or the assistant commander of the police station. I remained doing that until 1992. When the war broke out from the Public Security Service, I was transferred to the State Security Service, and I remained working there from April 1992 until the 1st of June 1998 when I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us a brief description of your jobs and the possible distinction between the Public Security Service and the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e. when the Ministry of the Interior Republika Srpska was established, it had the Public Security Service and the State Security Service. The Public Security Service was engaged on policing, which concerned the protection of personal security of citizens, controlling peace and order, controlling traffic, and other such jobs which fell within the purview of police. The State Security Service was the other segment of the interior, which was involved in intelligence and counterintelligence, as all any other intelligence and counterintelligence service in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the war, as I can see, you were engaged in the state security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please briefly explain the organisational structure of the state security sector within the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The State Security Service when it was established within the Ministry of the Interior Republika Srpska was first known as the National Security Service; and then in a subsequent period, I believe that it was -- either in 1993 or 1994 it was renamed and became the Sector of State Security within the Ministry of the Interior. The State Security Service or the National Security Service was organised on the territorial principle, and it had several centres across the country. I worked in the centre of state security in Serbian Sarajevo, which was also organised or broken down into smaller departments in the territory of several municipalities. I worked in the detachment of the state security headquartered in Sokolac, which covered the municipalities of Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Rogatica, and parts of the municipalities of Olovo and Srpska Gorazde, which were under the control of the Army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The places that you have just mentioned, were they under the territorial jurisdiction of your detachment and were they bordering on the territories that were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Our detachment covered those areas which bordered on the frontlines facing the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can thus tell you that from Gorazde, across the territory of the municipality of Rogatica, Han Pijesak, and Olovo, those were all border areas that had a direct contact with the frontline facing the army of Bosnian Muslims or the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the discharge of the your duties that fell within your purview, did you cooperate or did you have contact with the similar service in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the war broke out and the Army Republika Srpska was established, we first established contacts with our colleagues from the public security stations on the ground and then with our colleagues from the military security, which existed in the areas where particular brigades were headquartered. By and large, this cooperation was maintained with security officers or people who were involved in similar jobs as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some names, the names of those security officers with whom you cooperated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: At first, those were the officers in the brigade commands. I can mention a few; for example, Mr. Popovic, who was the security officer in the second Romanija brigade. In the Rogatica brigade, the security officer was the one with whom we cooperated, and then later on I met some colleagues from the security administration, in Similjaka [phoen], for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to meet Mr. Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the occasion? Why did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, but I believe that this was towards the end of 1993. I had some contacts with junior officers, and that's how I got in touch with their superior, Mr. Beara, and it was all about exchanging certain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what was the topic of those discussions and meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the topic of our discussions and meetings -- or rather, mostly this was all about exchanging information that had to do with any operational intelligence that would indicate that there was a possibility of an infiltration of sabotage groups or Muslim armed formations into the territory that was in the municipalities controlled by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, was there any overlap in the jurisdictions between your service and the military service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no overlap as far as I could see. Their basic task was intelligence work along the frontlines, or rather, in the combat zones; whereas what we were doing had to do with the territory inside, in the depth where there was no fighting and where there were municipal authorities of the Republika Srpska operating normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us some examples, some occasions where you did this work in your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many such occasions, particularly in 1992, once the war broke out. Well, it was a long time ago, 15 years ago, but I do remember some striking examples of some events where a large number of Serb civilians were casualties. So let me start with the municipality of Rogatica. I recall an event in the village - I think it was called Vodice - where four members of the Obradovic family were killed. A girl by the name of Danijela Obradovic was wounded, raped, and then her throat was slit. I remember the murder from an ambush of two civilians travelling in a passenger vehicle. I think it was Radenko Bjevakovic and his daughter Sonja. Again, in the Rogatica municipality in the village of Kukavice, sometime in August 1992 when the Serb population was expelled from the municipal of Gorazde, as the civilians were withdrawing in a column, there was an attack on this column and several civilians were killed; dozens were wounded; a bus was set on fire as were many passenger cars. Then in Han Pijesak, again, at the beginning of the war in 1992, June, July, there was an attack on the village of Borovine and Jelovice. Several civilians were killed; several buildings were set on fire. I remember that Marko Borovina and his son who was disabled - he couldn't walk - they were killed in the house; they were set on fire. I also recall the killing of civilians in the village of Mislova between Han Pijesak and Rogatica. The murder occurred when people were doing farm work. In Sokolac, sometime in the summer of 1992, the village of Poratak was set on fire. Several civilians were wounded. I also a remember a mass murder in the village of Turcine where a Muslim family was killed much. It was in the Sokolac municipality. As far as I can remember, I was on the commission that carried out the onsite investigation, and we analysed the situation and put together a file. I believe that a criminal report was filed against unidentified perpetrators as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please explain to us this: You told us that you did the onsite investigation. What was the composition of the team, and how -- what was the procedure once the onsite investigation was completed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Once we learned about this incident in which this Muslim family was killed, the procedure was to set up a commission to carry out the onsite investigation headed by the investigating judge of the municipal court in Sokolac. There were crime -- there was a crime scene technician and I, as the representative of the National Security Service. We went there to the crime scene. The onsite investigation was led by the investigating judge. I think it was a murder of four members of a single family and two members of another family who were visiting. After the onsite investigation, the bodies were brought to the military hospital in Romanija, and there was a autopsy. And since they did not have any close relatives, they were buried in the compound of the military hospital. After that, the procedure was to file a criminal report with the municipal public prosecutor, who then had to take other operative measures in order to identify and locate the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So in other words, this was the usual procedure when you were dealing with those cases?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if we received information on time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I don't know if you followed the plight of repeal of the interpreters. You've been overlapping, both of you, so if you could kindly pause between question and answer. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I got a little bit carried away. First I warned the witness, and then I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, when was the first time that you had an opportunity to work together with the military security organs to investigate the crimes that were committed during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in mid-August 1995 as far as I can remember. There was a dispatch informing me that I have to report to the Foca penitentiary and correctional facility, where there is a certain number of prisoners of war from the Zepa Muslim brigade, and that a team was set up to investigate the matter, to investigate the matter of any war crimes that may have been committed. And this information was to be obtained by questioning those prisoners of war. I received this dispatch from my immediate superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recall, how was this joint commission set up, or rather, who were the representatives of this commission, or rather, what organs did they represent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, when I left there and reported there pursuant to the dispatch that I received, I encountered a certain number of operations officers from the Public Security Service there in Foca. They were from the crime police. They were in charge of dealing with crimes against humanity, and there were also some officers from the security administration. After that, we all had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did anyone chair this commission? How did this commission work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, I think Officer Spiro Pereula introduced himself. He was the coordinator of this team. He was there on behalf of the security administration, and I remember that this meeting was attended, also, by the military prosecutors and the military investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I was wondering if we could just have the name, the last name of the individual. I heard it, but it wasn't transcribed. I'm not sure if I heard it correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking of Spiro something, and could we have the names again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Spiro Pereula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that make sense to you, Mr. Thayer, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I thank my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is spelled a little bit wrongly, but I think that we all heard it and will be able to remember it. The name is Pereula. It's not what it says here, but I think we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That shouldn't be a problem. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, could you please explain to me, how did this commission work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting, it was stated for the record that the officers from the security administration, the operations officers from the public security stations bordering with the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica, people who had some operational intelligence already about war crimes against the civilian population were present there in the commission; and I was there, too, representing the State Security Service because I also dealt with the area or I covered the area that gravitated towards the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica. After the meeting, we broke up in smaller groups of two, and we started conducting preliminary interviews with the prisoners of war who were detained in the correctional and penitentiary facility in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who told you that those were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I received the dispatch and the order to go there, to Foca, the dispatch said that there was a certain number of prisoners of war from the Zepa area in the KP Dom penitentiary and correctional facility on Foca, and probably somewhere at the higher levels of my State Security Service and the security administration this agreement had been reached earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let us go back to the questioning, to the procedure. Could you please tell us, what do you recall, what were the conditions in the course of these interviews or questioning, and what was the first thing that you learned in the course of those interviews?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the people were questioned in separate rooms and offices where there were two operations officers per room. One would be a security officer, and the other one would be from the security service. The interviews were carried out in a very correct and professional manner. There was no coercion at all, and I also noticed that the prisoners of war that were questioned were in good mental and physical condition. Through those preliminary interviews, some operational intelligence was obtained, and for the most part this was intelligence that had to do with the whole 285th Zepa Brigade between 1.300 and 1.500 [Realtime transcript read in error, "103.000 and 105.000"] members of this brigade who, after the civilians had left Zepa from the area controlled by the BH Army, refused to hand over their military weapons, withdrew to the Igrisnik sector, and decided that a large number of soldiers should surrender to the army of Yugoslavia after crossing the Drina river into the territory of the Republic of Serbia and that a certain number should cross into the territory held by the BH Army by launching an attempt to break through the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to clarification for the number that's in the transcript for the 285th Zepa Brigade. I suspect that it's incorrect. I just wanted to clarify the record. My friends, I think, agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. I would tend to agree with Mr. Thayer here. If you could clarify it with the witness. It's probably a translation error. Let's go through it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, could you please repeat. What information did you get about the strength of how many soldiers were there because it says 103.000 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In the interviews, we obtained the intelligence that up to 1.500 soldiers of the Zepa Brigade had withdrew to the Igrisnik area where a decision was made that those who wanted to do so could cross into the territory of Yugoslavia - cross the Drina river, in other words - and surrender to the Yugoslav army. Somewhere between 800 and 1.000 soldiers opted for that, and between 4 and 500 soldiers decided to do a break-through through the territory of Republika Srpska along the access leading to Kladanj, Gorazde, and Orilla [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You obtained this information based on the questioning of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we got it from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to use a document. The number is 2D24 -- 2D524. Because the documentation is rather voluminous, I would like to -- we did just a draft version of the translation, so I would like the usher to hand the draft version of the translation to the Bench and the Prosecution, and I will be dealing with this document in Serbian. Can we please see the third page of the document. Scroll down a little, please. Let's see who drafted the document and who signed it. We can see in the left bottom, it says in Uzice on 8 of March 1996, and in the right corner it says OZSUP Uzice, and let me translate this as the secretariat of the interior. And let's go back to page 1, please. Thank you. In the right-hand side corner, it says that the copy of the document is identical to the original. The name of the person who certifies that is Predrag Vojicic, and this was done on the 18th of July, 2007, and there is a stamp of the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade, which is in the Republic of Serbia. The title of the document is information about the conditions of life and stay of the most members in the reception centres in Mitrovo Polje and Branesko Polje. Before I continue reading the document, I would like to inform you that we received the document from the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal of the Republic of Serbia, and we received that together with some other documents. The document has a total of three pages. I don't have to read all of it. I've just singled out the relevant portions. At the very beginning, it says:

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Somebody's mobile phone must be switched on, and it is virtually impossible to listen to anybody in the courtroom speaking because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please, I'm not in a position, of course, to know who has got his or her mobile switched on. Could you all check and make sure that if you are carrying a mobile phone, it's switched off. And I also ask all the other booths, technicians and interpreters, to do the same because sometimes we can hear phones ringing. The noise that we have is still being received, so we've been complaining about it for the past ten minutes or so. Let's carry on. In the meantime, please check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is, as judge Prost is saying, I mean, we can continue to live with it and proceed; but if it's disturbing the interpreter's work to an extent that they cannot continue, we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but please do let us know if it's becoming too much for you because we do understand how difficult and how problematic it can become.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do let us know when we can continue. We can continue? No. All right. Let's give it a try. Seems to be better, at least now for the time being. Let's proceed. Yes, Mr. Nikolic. Please just check that you are on the right channel, you are switched on on the right channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is information about the conditions of a life and stay of the MOS [Realtime transcript read in error, "most"] members in Mitrovo Polje and Branesko Polje reception centres between 31st of July and 25 October 1995. Having violated the state border of the SRJ, smaller and bigger groups of MOS members entered the territory of the state from the Zepa territory. There were a total of 799 persons during that. They crossed the state border in the territory of the village of Jagostica in the municipality of Bajina Basta from the direction of Crni Potok, i.e., from the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. They crossed the Drina River in Bojs [phoen], improvised rafts and other such things. The media informed the general public about the arrival of those groups. We would like to note that the violation of the territory of our state were carried out by two armed groups, which through illegal channels managed to cross over into the territory of Sandzak. The accommodation of the MOS [Realtime transcript read in error, "mosque"] members was provided into reception centres, one in Branesko Polje in Cerite [phoen] municipality and Mitrovo Polje at Goc. The reception centre in Branesko Polje was established on the 1st of August 1995, in the workers' barracks of Planum and on Mitrovo Polje on the 1st of August in the MUP holiday camp. As soon as the reception centres were established, the MKSK was informed about that, which is the International Red Cross Committee, the UNHCR, and other international organizations; and most members were given a partial refugee status. I will stop here for a moment. I believe that it will be useful for us to explain the abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that my colleague is about to clarify what I was going to mention because page 15, line 16; page 15, line 25; and page 16, line 7, we see an abbreviation that was used MOS, and I believe that the witness will clarify this because as we see it now on the transcript we read "mosque," "most," and "most." But it will be clarified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Nikolic, please attend to that, and Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, I hope you have the text that I've just read out before you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and expand the abbreviation "MOS," MOS.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation "MOS" stands for the Muslim Armed Forces, which mean that those were Muslim soldiers, i.e., members of the 285 Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And could you also expand the abbreviation "MUP," MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation MUP stands for the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, can we please look at page 3 of the same document. Thank you very much. This is what I need. Paragraph 3 from the top of the page, I will read: "Between the 7th of December 1995 and today, several MOS members were allowed to move into third countries so that a total of 495 of them have left up to date. Of that number, 240 moved to the United States; 103 moved to Australia; 11 to Sweden; 78 to France; 36 to Ireland; 10 to the Netherlands; 12 to Switzerland; and 31 to Finland." Further on in the text, it says, "We note that three members of the MOS died in our territory: one of them from the border to the reception centre in Branesko Polje, another one in the reception centre in Branesko Polje, and the third one died in the reception centre in Mitrovo Polje. We also note that on the 9th of February, 1996, that MOS members from the reception centre in Mitrovo Polje were all transferred to the reception centre in Branesko Polje, and now the total number amounts to 301." Mr. Vojinovic, I have shown you this document, and I would like to ask you whether this illustrates what you have just told us based on the information that you had received from the detainees in the Foca prison.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely the document that confirms what I learned during that period of time, i.e., that all the members of the 285th Zepa Brigade had withdrawn. They had not surrendered their weapons, and the number that I mentioned, anything between 800 and 1.000 soldiers that crossed over to Yugoslavia, is actually 700 soldiers, and this document just confirms information that we obtained through our work during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go back to those detainee interviews. While you were interviewing the detainees, did you come by any concrete information about the crimes that had been committed in the times preceding the interviews?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: During the detainee interviews, we also came by some concrete information, which only confirmed that a certain number of the members of the Zepa Brigade had, indeed, committed several crimes against humanity and the international law in the territory of Republika Srpska; i.e., they had killed a few civilians and torched several facilities or villages. Also, in the course of those interviews, we came by information that immediately prior to the fall of Zepa, i.e., prior to the armed conflict between the Army Republika Srpska and the members of the 285th Brigade in Zepa, and in the territory of Republika Srpska towards the end of June 1995, pursuant to the order of the second corps of the BiH army, eight larger sabotage groups had been infiltrated into that territory from Zepa. Their mission was to carry out several combat operations on the Sokolac-Vlasenici road in order to engage the Serb forces and move them away from Sarajevo. In the course of the -- those operations, a few civilians [as interpreted] and a few members of the Army of Republika Srpska had been killed. As a result of that, the Army of Republika Srpska had embarked on the disarming of the members of the 285th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are a bit concerned, Your Honour, about the translation as to the number of civilians. I don't want to lead in relation to this. Perhaps the witness could be asked again what adjective he used in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is no harm in leading at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't think he said "a few civilians." I'm told he used a different adjective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could you follow -- of course, we couldn't follow the witness in his original language, but Mr. Nikolic certainly must have. So perhaps you can clarify that having heard Mr. Josse, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the witness to repeat what he has just told us about the information that they had obtained about the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What concrete information did you receive from the prisoners about the civilians that had been killed during those operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: During those interviews we learned, which was later on confirmed, i.e., certain perpetrators were identified. Those who had been involved in the killing of the civilians in the village of Borovine in 1995, the killing of the civilian Stojan Veljovic, the killings of several [as interpreted] civilians in the village of Visnjici in the territory of the Milici municipality, and I really cannot remember any more specific details because I don't have any documents to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is an error in transcript. At the page 19, line 24, the B/C/S word "vise" was translated as "several."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how should it be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As more civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway -- but I think I heard Mr. Zivanovic say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Many civilians." It should be translated as "many civilians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the difference between "many" and "several"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. I am not a native English speaker, but I don't think it makes much difference at this stage. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, as a result of those interviews, were any criminal reports filed? Who did that, if so, and which organ or body received those criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: After conducting preliminary interviews with all the persons who were detained in the Foca correctional and penitentiary facility, the security administration of the Army of Republika Srpska filed several criminal reports against several persons with the military Prosecutor's Office. I can't recall the exact number of those criminal reports and the crimes that this referred to, but the crimes were crimes against humanity and crimes against international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to see Document 2D528. We received this document from the witness himself, and the only thing that you will see is the first name in the English translation. Could the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber please be handed the draft version of the translation. I don't think that it will be difficult to follow the rest of the document because all we are interested in is the number of persons. In the left upper corner of this document, it says, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Security and Intelligence Sector, security administration, strictly confidential. There's no number, and the date is the 23rd of August, 1995. It is addressed to the basic military Prosecutor's Office in Bijeljina. It says in the text, "Pursuant to Articles 150 and 151, para 1, of the Law on Criminal Procedure, a criminal report is hereby filed against the following persons." The person that is listed under number 1 is Mohmedalije Cavcic, and we have his personal details. I will now ask whether we should now go into private session because we will now be dealing with the personal details of some persons, and perhaps it would be good not to have this made public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we please move the document up a little bit so that we can see who issued this document. So in the lower right-hand corner it says, "The government, Deputy Prime Minister Bozidar Djelic," and there is a stamp, "the Government of the Republic of Serbia, Belgrade." Could you please move the document up a little bit. The first section in the upper left-hand corner, it says "confidential," and then it says in the text, Pursuant to Article 11 of the law on the cooperation of Serbia and Montenegro with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, cooperation of the International Tribunal for the criminal prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia from 1992. It is published in the official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in number 18/02 and the official Gazette of the SCG, the number is 16/03, and Article 43, para 3, of the law on the government, published in the official Gazette of the RS. Number 55/05, 71/05, and the correction in 101/07, the government issues the following conclusion: Attorney-At-Law Predrag Nikolic, an investigator in the Defence team of Ljubisa Beara, is allowed to submit documents attached to the present conclusion submitted in the attachment to memorandum sent by the Ministry of the Interior, 01, number 5940/07-9 of the 4th of January, 2008. And para 2 reads as follows: "The conclusion is to be sent to the international --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you want to prove with this because, I mean, if there is anyone who is going to doubt the authenticity of this document, I would be very surprised; and secondly, it speaks for itself. It doesn't need to be read out in court, does it? We can all read it. We have already done so, so we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, attached to this conclusion is a list of statements of 105 persons who provided those statements, and the statements were submitted together with this document. That's what I wanted to do. I wanted to tender this into evidence in order to be able to tender the following document, which is 2D422. Could the draft translation of this document into English, Document 2D422, be provided to the Bench and the Prosecution. The title of this document is "Record," and I would now like us to move into private session so that I could read the name and personal details of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number is 2D526. We have a draft English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I am tempted to ask the question to the Prosecution. If Mr. Nikolic had, instead of taking two hours of our time, just presented these documents and asked if the Prosecution contested any of this stuff here, what would have been your answer, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to a certain extent we, as we have said on numerous occasions, do not contest the general proposition that there were sabotage acts and other acts committed by forces from within both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclave from within the enclaves outwards. With respect to these particular statements, without having been given more information about what was going to be the nature of the examination, it would have been difficult for me to stipulate. However, had it simply been put to me that these documents are X, Y, and Z, we may very well have stipulated that they are simply reports without going into the authenticity or the conditions under which the alleged statements were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nikolic, please proceed and try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My examination is drawing to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by the military court in Bijeljina as you can see in the heading. The number is SU 128/2000 dated 19 July 2000. It refers to the list of cases transferred onto the basic court in Rogatica. Under Item number 1, KI-4798/95 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, please, Mr. Nikolic, you don't need to read to us or to the witness the contents of a document. We can read it ourselves. I take it that the witness has already seen this document. Go to the question, please, because we if we stay reading each document that we get here, we'll be here for the next four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, my question is this: All these documents that we have seen here today, do they all refer to what you learned during your wartime investigations and during your interviews with the prisoners in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are precisely documents of that nature, documents which confirm all of our previous knowledge and add to that some new information obtained in order to identify the perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before I conclude my examination-in-chief, I'll go back to the part of your testimony during which you spoke about the persons and officers from the security services with whom you cooperated; and within that context, you mentioned the accused Colonel Ljubisa Beara. This was a long time ago, but I would still like to ask you to describe to the best of your recollection the way he looked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubisa Beara remains in my recollection as a person who was tall, with receding -- with a receding hairline, grey hair. He sported spectacles, rather heavily built, and he also spoke with a specific dialect that was reminiscent of the Ikavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You had several opportunities to meet with Mr. Beara. What were your impressions of him as an officer and a soldier of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I perceived Mr. Beara as an officer who performed his duties, the duties from within the purview of security in a professional manner, in a very responsible manner. During our conversations, he also showed a sense of humour so that my time spent with the gentleman in question was rather pleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This brings my examination-in-chief to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Now, Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony so far, you have also told us that while working in the state security of the Ministry of the Interior, you also cooperated with the military security of the 2nd Romanija Brigade and that you met Mr. Vujadin Popovic at the time. Let me first ask you whether you can tell us - if you remember, of course - until when did you have regular contacts with Mr. Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I cooperated with Mr. Vujadin Popovic, and we had a very good relationship and very good professional contacts. Before he joined the Romanija Brigade, for a year or year and a half he was the security officer in the 2nd Romania Brigade, or rather, that's when we cooperated, when he was the security officer in the 2nd Romanija Brigade for a year or a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that time while you had regular contacts with him, did you or the service that you were a member of, did you receive any orders from him? Did there come a time when you were subordinated either to him personally or to the military security service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Our cooperation was mutually beneficial, but the military security service did not have any jurisdiction whatsoever over any other security service, either the Public Security Service or the State Security Service. They did not have any jurisdiction over either the former or the latter. Our superior was the ministry of the interior of Republika Srpska, and that ministry was responsible for our work and for the coordination of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now play a video recording. It's a very short clip, 4 minutes, and it shows Vujadin Popovic too. So I would like you to look at it and tell us whether you can recall this event and if you do, to tell us something about it. It's 1D 1310.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The drama of the Croat refugees from Vares continues. The poor people have sought salvation from the Muslim soldiers, their erstwhile allies in the Serb territory. The question now is where to go next. Many of them don't want to go to either Herceg-Bosna or Croatia. I wanted to avoid Kiseljak. That's why I headed to this territory, to Sokolac, to be able to leave for Herzegovina as soon as possible if I have to. We are trying to avoid going from hill to hill. That's what it is. Herceg-Bosna representatives are offering accommodation in Kiseljak, but some of them would like to seek shelter in Serbia and Montenegro. I want to go to Subotica. I have four brothers-in-law in Subotica. I think that the Serb people there will let me go there." "Were you scared as they moved towards the Serb territory?" "I was not scared. I was only scared of the Muslims. I'm going to Belgrade." "And you are not scared of going to Belgrade?" "We've lived along Serbs for centuries and never had any problems, and this war was not started by Serbs. The refugees from Vares now recall their links with Serbia, asking themselves why this happened to them, resentful of their leadership. No one is taking care of us. They have all fled the lines. They have fled. Here they are, and my husband was the first to stay down there and fight, and all those municipal officials and leaders, they're all over the place, skulking in camps. Can you believe it? For sure, and look where they got us, into this mud, and they all wanted to do something. They gave us rice full of weevils and sold the rest. Who did they sell it to? They sold it in shops. The stuff went to Tuzla, too, into Tuzla, all for Tuzla. It all went to Tuzla. Whole convoys went. A convoy would come, and the trucks from Tuzla took everything away. Just the message for the Serb people: Watch out for UNPROFOR because they, in fact, play the main role in Vares, stirred things up?" "As the ordeal of these people continues, a lot of things are now seen in the different light than before. The Serb people have taken them in just as they have always helped those in need. The very way in which the people in the Republika Srpska army took them in has given them some feeling of safety, their personal safety and that of their families. They would probably like to feel the same way when they cross over. "The exodus of the Croatian people from Vares area has continued. Only in the last four days, as long as the fighting between Croats and Muslims in this area has gone on, over 5.000 civilians from Vares and the environs have fled into the Serb territory. Columns of buses, trucks, and cars full of women, children, and the elderly have fled the Muslim warriors and sought shelter and aid from the Serb fighters, and Serbs help those in trouble if they can. "Yet again, they have taken the Croats from Vares Inn, fed them, and escorted them in an organised fashion across the Serb territory and the border crossing at Kobiljaca to Kiseljak, according to our intelligence, and it is reliable, since the Republika Srpska army has done this job extremely properly and humanely. It has taken in the women, the children, the infirmed, the elderly, the wounded, et cetera, and transferred them to Kiseljak. We are talking about more than 5.000 people. The last convoy is due today, and we will do it too. On the 7th of November, we are going to Sokolac. From Sokolac, we will move 1.000 women and children, again, to Kiseljak. I don't know of any similar examples of any Croat soldiers doing what my soldiers, members of the Republika Srpska army, have done over the past, let's say, four months as the fighting between co-ac and Muslims intensified and this conflict in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina has culminated. All men of military age ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, I would like to ask you this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to let the video finish before objecting. I have two objections, and I understand that the practice is to permit the question to be asked first, but -- and we're in sort of a bind sometimes when we do that. But I have two objections, really. One is, we don't know as far as I can see what year this film apparently -- allegedly was filmed, and I'd like an idea of what the relevance of this line of questioning that we are about to hear is, how it arises from the examination of this witness, before we take more time going into events which don't seem particularly relevant or relevant completely to 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one. What time frame does this video clip refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'd like to say that this video was disclosed by the Prosecution as Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's still -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it is related to the events in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: '93. Okay. And let's hear what your questions are, and if we have any concerns about relevance, of course, we will intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to Rule 68, I do not see any reason to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, don't -- let's hear the questions, and if we can figure out that they could be relevant, they could be irrelevant. But we have to hear them first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question for you, Mr. Vojinovic is, do you remember this event? Do you have any knowledge of this event, and can you tell us something about it and Vujadin Popovic's participation in this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this event well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding is that my friend has closed his evidence and this is, in any event, irrelevant. It's 1993. It's an event that is not further described than what's going on in the video. I just don't see how this is relevant and how it flows from this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's wait to hear the other questions, I think, because if they are related it can help us decide better. The fact that we are talking of 1993 doesn't necessarily exclude relevance, but let's hear the other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I have put the question to the witness. Is it permitted or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. For the time being, let's proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm expecting his answer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did answer. He said, yes, I remember this event very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, can you tell us now, what is it that you remember from this period about this event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I remember this event so clearly because I was able to recognise the site where the refugees from the Vares area were housed on this video clip. They were all ethnic Croats - that's Brezjak, near Sokolac - where the UNHCR sometime in June 1992 set up a tent camp to house this refugees, civilians of Serb ethnic background who managed to flee from areas controlled by the Bosnian army, from central Bosnia, Zenica, Kakanj, and so on, to the Serb-controlled territory, and this was the first camp where they were taken in. They were given some food, and then they went on according to their own wishes. This camp was full at all times. It is my evaluation that between 200 and 250 refugees remained there, but they would stay there two, three, seven days at the most, and then they would go on. When the war between Muslims and Croats broke out, when Vares where the majority of the population was Croat, when it was attacked by Muslim armed formations, the civilians, Croats, lest they should find themselves in an encirclement, lest they should find themselves in any kind of threat from the Muslims, they decided to cross into the territory of the Republika Srpska. This was decided at a higher level. I know that our troops, the Republika Srpska army, took part in transporting those people, feeding them, assisting to feed them, and to put them up in the tent camp in Sokolac. I know that at that time we had some tasks that had to do with the security, personal security, and the security of property of the civilians in that camp. I remember that the military security was also involved; i.e., Mr. Vujadin Popovic, he had some tasks in providing security for those civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Could you please tell me, in the course of your contacts with Mr. Vujadin Popovic, did you ever feel any animosity on his part towards other ethnic groups, Croats, Muslims, or any other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary was the case, in fact. In his conversations with me, I never felt any animosity on his part towards other ethnic groups except for the armed formations of the enemy side, Muslims, Croats in the battle field on the separation line on the front lines, but that's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vojinovic. [In English] No more questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic, do you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Nikolic informed the Trial Chamber that the Nikolic Defence team do not wish to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Lazarevic? You had requested 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I indicated, I believe, that we'll have ten minutes or maybe we won't have any cross-examination, if any, and we decided not to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Ms. Fauveau, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Gvero Defence team don't wish to cross-examine this witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes, do you wish to cross-examine this witness? You have asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not that long. One or two questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, earlier this morning you were telling about your involvement in the investigation of the murder of a Muslim family in 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were involved in that investigation as part of your role within the National Security Service. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you told us that the investigation was headed by an investigative judge. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. He was the head of the onsite investigation. That was the Judge of the municipal court in Sokolac because it was their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's quite correct. What I really want to know from you is, who would have instructed him to carry out that investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he received any orders or not, but the usual practice in accordance with the law in criminal procedure, which was enforced at that time, was once information came in that the crime was committed or that an incident had taken place, once this information comes in, it usually came in via the duty desk of the police stations, and they were duty-bound to inform the investigative judge, the duty investigative judge, and the investigative judge then issued an order, or rather, verbally requested a vehicle from the MUP and also personnel qualified to carry out an onsite investigation; in other words, crime scene technicians, crime police inspector, in order to find and secure evidence on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you know whether that is what happened in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes because I was a member of this commission representing the State Security Service. That's exactly what happened. A commission was set up. It was headed by the investigative judge. It included the crime scene technician, a crime police inspector, and myself, and we went to the crime scene in two vehicles. There were also some other police officers who were there to, first of all, ensure that the members of the commission were safe and also to secure the perimeter around the scene because the house where this crime was committed, where there was this multiple murder of the Muslim family, was located in such a way that there was a forest nearby; and this is where the armed Muslim groups passed from Rogatica towards Zepa and Srebrenica. And when information came in about this event, it was clear that the safety of the commission during the onsite investigation might be compromised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I've got no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Haynes. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to give you an idea, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had asked for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think I may be able to finish by the break at 12.30. I'll do my best, but it's not going to be an hour and a half from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, which means, Madam Registrar, the next witness should remain available, all right? And we'll start him immediately after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Morning, sir. We've not met. My name is Nelson Thayer, and I will be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, it's fair to say that the events immediately following the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa in terms of the break-through of military-aged men from those two enclaves, that was something of intense interest to security and intelligence organs both on the military side and the civilian side like yourself; isn't that correct? Isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you already told us about the cooperation between the army's security and intelligence organs and the state security organs. I want to focus your attention on July of 1995 to begin with and ask you about your contacts with certain individuals and just see what you recall about your interactions with them, if any, in July of 1995. And just to save time, if you don't recall particular contacts in July of 1995, but you did have contacts with the individual, could you describe what those contacts were, okay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. In July --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me make things easier for you, and I'll just go through some names, okay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, Colonel Beara: Did you have contacts with him in July of 1995 following the fall of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any contacts with Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And prior to July of 1995, what was your most recent contact with him that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I can't remember when it was before this time period. For the most part, I had contacts with lower ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood. Well, do you recall any contacts with him in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall the exact date and time, but I first met Mr. Beara sometime in late 1993, and during the war I may have met him just a couple of times in informal settings, and I remember that the last time I met him was sometime in 1996. There was some kind of ceremonial lunch, some kind of a feast to celebrate something. Those are the occasions that I remember regarding meeting Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So is it fair to say, then, that your contacts were not prolonged or frequent with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. How about an individual named Dragomir Pecanac Do you recall having contact with him? He was a major serving under Colonel Beara in the security administration. Do you remember Major Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him from the wartime, but I did not cooperate closely with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as we go through some of the other parts of the chain of command, do you recall having contacts with Svetozar Kosoric from the Drina Corps on the intelligence side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never met Mr. Kosoric at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about at the brigade level? Did you have contact in July of 1995 with the commander of the Rogatica Brigade; that would be Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, not. I was not in contact with Mr. Kusic, but throughout the war I was in contact with his security officer, and our relationship and our cooperation were extremely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that security officer's name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Captain Zoran Carkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to turn your attention to the individuals that were listed on the document that my friend showed you of individuals who had been captured in Serbia and interrogated there. You recall being shown a document that had a list of over a hundred people, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall the document, or I saw the list, the criminal report against 149 persons who were reported because there were grounds for suspicion that they had committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so it's clear for the record, sir, is it your testimony that those individuals were transferred to the prison in Foca where they were then, again, interrogated; or is it your testimony that when you interviewed prisoners at Foca, they either talked about the individuals on that list or referred to acts that you considered were connected to those individuals on that list of prisoners from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the conversations or interviews with the prisoners in Foca, as far as I can recall there were about 35 of them. Based on their statements obtained in the course of those interviews, we learned on the basis of what they told us that a certain number of persons for whom there were indicators that they had committed war crimes, that they had crossed into the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and that they were somewhere there in Serbia. I didn't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in coming to some of the conclusions that you made today concerning the evidence that certain individuals had participated in what you called war crimes or crimes against humanity, you relied on the information that came to you from the Serbian authorities, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the authorities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. We did not rely on the documents that you have, documents issued in the territory of Serbia. We relied on our previous knowledge, the intelligence we gathered throughout the war about the acts, the crimes, the victims, and the perpetrators; but from the prisoners in Foca, we obtained information that confirmed with what we knew already, or we obtained knowledge that we didn't have before, but we learned from them that some people for whom there were grounds for suspicion that they crossed to Serbia and some others had managed to break through under arms through the territory of Republika Srpska to the BH Army-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were aware, were you not, that there was a group of approximately 40 military-aged men and some older men from the Zepa area who were held in a prison farm in Rogatica during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that a certain number of persons from Zepa were held in the prison in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that location was the - forgive my pronunciation - the Rasadnik farm?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that was the name of the facility, and the facility was located at a place as you are leaving the town of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, it's just outside the town of Rogatica, is it not? And if you would, just orient the Trial Chamber to what direction outside of the town of Rogatica this farm was located.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This farm was still in the town, but as you leave town going towards Sokolac, that's where you will find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, and just to save us from having to pull out a map, Sokolac is to the west of Rogatica, northwest, south?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: North of Rogatica, at some 30 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this farm, do you recall what type of farm it was? Was it an agricultural farm? Was it used for raising cattle, or can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war it was an agricultural farm, but during the war it was not operational. As far as I can remember, there was an administrative building there, which was used as a war prison for the temporary accommodation of prisoners of war. From there, they were then exchanged and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Who ran that farm, sir, the army or MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the warden was an individual named Zoran Neskovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember the names. I would go there only occasionally, maybe every two or three months, if I had to see a prisoner. There was always some other member of security, so I really wouldn't be able to tell you who the warden was or who the soldiers providing security were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in terms of the guards, sir, many of those guards, perhaps all of them, were actually policemen from the Rogatica area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but they were all soldiers of the VRS, but I don't know which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall interviewing any of the prisoners that were held in this farm prison in Rogatica in July of 1995 during the course of this investigation that you told the Trial Chamber about earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and this was 15 years ago, I believe that before I left for Foca I conducted an interview over there with Handija Torlak, if I'm not mistaken. He was the president of the executive board of the war presidency of Zepa. I remember the interview with that person, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were at the prison, do you recall that with Mr. Torlak was a man named Mehmed Hajdic [phoen] who was the hodja of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know that there were several men from Zepa held in custody, but I remember Mr. Torlak because he had been in a political position in Zepa, in the war presidencies there. That's why I remember the interview during which he was very fair, and he provided a very accurate description of what was going on in and around Zepa at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall an individual also being present with Mr. Torlak by the name of Amir Imamovic, who was the head of civil protection from Zepa, somebody in whom I presume you would have been interested at the time to interview?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember the name. It doesn't ring any bells. I only remember Mr. Torlak because at the time we really wanted to talk to somebody from the leadership and to obtain information. We were interested in information about the armed formations that crossed our territory and in certain ways threatened the security of the civilian population and the villages that they had to go through. That's why we were most interested in obtaining that information and providing protection to these villages that were endangered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this period of time, sir, the name of Avdo Palic was certainly known to you was the commander of the Zepa Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you recall, do you not, that Colonel Palic was captured by Serb forces and held shortly after the transportation of the civilian population of Zepa, the men, women -- older men, women, and children had been completed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what you know about the interrogation process of Colonel Palic and the circumstances surrounding his detention during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise? I don't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what you know about what happened to Colonel Palic after he was taken into Serb custody in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Colonel Palic was detained in Zepa because he was the responsible commander of the 285th Brigade and he did not comply with the agreement on the surrender of his soldiers, and according to that agreement they should have been exchanged on the all-for-all principle; i.e., members of his brigade should have been exchanged for the Serb soldiers that were held by BH Army. When he was captured, he was taken to a centre where he was going to be exchanged for high-ranking officer of the VRS. I don't know anything else about his fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you told us about how interested you would have been in interviewing Mr. Torlak, who you said was a civilian leader. You no doubt would have been intensely interested in what Colonel Palic had to say about the same issues about which you were interested in interviewing Mr. Torlak, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you present for any of the interviews, interrogations of Colonel Palic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber as best as you can when the interrogations began and who was present and where these interrogations precisely took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but I believe that it was either the end of July or the beginning of August. I had received a dispatch in my department in Sokolac telling me to go to the Borika Hotel in the municipality of Rogatica. There was supposed to be a prisoner there, and I was supposed to contact the security officer in the hotel who was to allow me to talk to the prisoner. I got into the car; I went there, to the Borika Hotel. I reported to an officer whose name I can't remember as I sit here, and the officer took me to one of the rooms. When I entered the room, I found three persons in there: two soldiers of the Republika Srpska army and a man in a camouflage American NATO uniform and boots, and they were sitting down facing each other. As I entered the room, the soldiers who provided the security for the prisoner left the room. I remained alone with the prisoner. When I asked him to identify himself, he identified himself as Avdo Palic, whom I had never seen before. I conducted an interview with him, and the interview lasted anything between and hour and a half and two hours. During the interview, Avdo was very correct in providing his statement. I remember well that he stated that the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and particularly Zepa and the troops of his brigade had been manipulated by the authorities in Sarajevo, that they had received orders on a new re-organisation, and that they would receive orders when to start breaking through towards Olovo and trying to link up with the other brigades of the BH Army. Since he was aware that Zepa had been proclaimed a protected and demilitarised area and that the demilitarisation had not been implemented and carried out, he just carried out orders that he had received from Sarajevo. He told me on that occasion that he personally in agreement with Zulfo Tursumovic from Srebrenica, the commander of one of the brigades of the 28th Division, had planned and carried out in June 1995 - I believe that it was on the 26th of June of that year - a total of nine sabotage operations during which several civilians and about 40 members of the Republika Srpska army had been killed, and also that on that occasion they captured a wounded Serb soldier and took him to Zepa. In that a same interview, Avdo explained to me that he had been a soldier and that he was duty-bound to carry out orders from Sarajevo, although he had known that this could result in a counteroffensive of the Republika Srpska army in order for them to protect their territory and their population. After the interview with the gentleman, I made an official note, which I forwarded to my service. A few days later, or a couple of days later, rather, I had another interview with the same gentleman about the same events, and on that occasion he personally confirmed to me and identified certain persons that had committed crimes. And after that second interview, I also compiled an official note, and about that time I received informal information that he was supposed to be exchanged for a high-ranking officer of Republika Srpska. From then on, I don't know what happened to him. Whether he was taken anywhere from that moment on, I don't know anything about his fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you described somebody being in what you called a NATO uniform and boots. Who was that person just so we are clear on the record?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: That person introduced himself to me as Avdo Palic. Since I had not met him before, I only took it for granted that he was the man that he claimed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say NATO unform, sir, just so we are clear, you are referring to a camouflage or design pattern. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, who was your immediate superior in the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
