utterances.text: The chief of the service was Tomislav Puhaljac, as far as I can remember. I hope I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom did he report, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: He reported to the chief of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July 1995, who was that person, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was Mr. Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So who gave you the order to go to the Hotel Borika?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who the person was, but I remember that a dispatch had arrived, or maybe it was a telephone call that I had. In any case, the order did arrive, and I carried it out the way it was spelled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you were aware, were you not, that the VRS had established a forward command post at the Hotel Borika?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was a forward command post. I believe that this is where soldiers were billeted, where they took their R and R.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the Hotel Borika, protocol would have required you to report to a VRS officer at that location, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a duty officer in the facility. I reported to the soldier at the entrance, who called him. I introduced myself to him. I told him what my mission was, and he enabled me to carry my mission out. I can't remember who the officer was or what unit he belonged to. I can't even remember what unit was billeted at that facility at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall who the highest ranking VRS officer was at that time in the Hotel Borika when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there were any high-ranking officers there. There were only lower-ranking officers together with a unit that was billeted there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 2793 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the computer screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Left or right?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It should be on the right for you, sir, and there should be an English translation on the left. Just take a moment, if you would, and acquaint yourself with this document, sir. Please let us know when we can scroll down to the bottom. Sir, we can see that this is a very urgent report from General Tolimir memorializing, according to the document, a conversation with Avdo Palic on 28 July 1995. Do you recall seeing General Tolimir in the Zepa area during this period of time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving any information at the time that General Tolimir was in fact in the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, and I really don't know why I should have been aware of the whereabouts of the high-ranking officers of the VRS at the time, where they were and where they were moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you knew what General Tolimir's position was, did you not, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You are identifying him as the assistant commander for security, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security of the Main Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. When you spoke with Colonel Palic, did you talk to him about the location of the minefields?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not talk to him about that. I spoke to Colonel Palic about the infiltration of his sabotage groups, what crimes they committed, when, and what were the consequences of those acts for the Serbian civil population, and also about the possible activities of his brigade in breaking through to Zepa because we wanted to have the timely information in order to protect the civilian population on the axis of these forces being pulled out and advancing towards Zepa and Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are a couple of minutes from the break. I'm going to move to a new document, so if we could take the break now, I think that would be most efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's take the break now, please, and it will be a 25-minute one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Let's pick up where we left off discussing this document that's on the screen. Do you recall whether this information was known to you or made known to you at the time that's contained in this report from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of this information, and this was not the topic of the discussion because I was not interested in anything that had to do with the military matters as indicated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 2790, please. 65 ter P 02790. You see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just take a moment and read it, please. Let us know when you are ready.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to see this document previously or the document that I just showed you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not had such an opportunity. These are military documents, so I have not had an opportunity to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, in this document dated 28 July 1995, and if we look at the report number, it directly follows the one prior, again, it's according to the latest information and describes where the communication centre for the Zepa Brigade is located. Is it your testimony still, sir, that this type of information was of no interest to you in your capacity as a state security officer in late July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Before this time, before the 28th of July, 1995, the service did have information that the Serbian brigade which was part of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the designation of the brigade. The interpreters didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, the interpreters didn't catch the name of the brigade. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the package radio system used by the 285 Zepa brigade, and it was able to establish direct contact with the command of the 28th Division and the 2nd corps of the BH Army as well as with the Main Staff of the BH Army; and they obtained direct orders via this communication system and was able to report directly to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it is the case, sir, is it not, that the State Security Service or -- and/or elements of the VRS were able to intercept communications among the Muslim forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And no doubt, this was information that was important to you during the war and which you received, reviewed, and relied upon during the course of your duties in the state security service; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was significant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what you know about the state security capabilities and operations to intercept the communications of the armija and/or its political leaders during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not know that because in the section where I worked we did not have the interception equipment, but we did have some knowledge obtained through some radio ham stations that were used, and information was obtained about the communication between Sarajevo and Zepa, or rather, the 2nd corps command and the Zepa Brigade command. This knowledge -- this information was mostly short, and some orders were relayed, and reports from the field were -- went the other way using the code book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just clarify your answer a bit, sir, when you refer to reports going the other way and using the code book. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you an example. For instance, from Sarajevo, they say that the Zepa Brigade command should ensure the reception of a packet under a certain number, which means that they have to provide personnel that would either receive armed personnel or some equipment and materiel that was being supplied to them at the time when Zepa was a demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what you are saying is this is information that was, in fact, intercepted by either army or state security operators and then passed on to, for example, yourself or people in your agency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to discuss a little bit more about what really was going on in mid-to late July 1995 as far as you and your agency were concerned, specifically when the breakout occurred from Srebrenica on or about the 11th, 12th of July, the column that everybody is familiar with, which headed for free territory. That was certainly information that was important to you to know. Even though it was moving in the opposite direction, this was information that was critical for you to know for your own security and intelligence purposes within your own agency; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, you could not say that because in that period I did not have any concrete activities, and I did not get any information about the events in Srebrenica and the developments around Srebrenica because Srebrenica was not adjacent to the area that I covered in operational terms. So I did not have any knowledge about those developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, tell the Court, then, when you first acquired knowledge that there was this column of thousands of Muslim men and boys and women that were headed in the direction of Zvornik at one point and posed a direct threat to Zvornik. When did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this on TV, in the media, in other words, and nothing more than that because when those units were pulled out from Srebrenica towards Tuzla, well, this is far from the area that I covered. The distance is about 100 kilometres, so we didn't have any obligations in this regard. There was no need for us to concern ourselves with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were familiar at the time, were you not, with Sinisa Glogovac and Vidomir Tomic, your colleagues in the State Security Service from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your testimony is that you did not know either of those individuals; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I did not encounter any of them. I didn't have any contacts with them, but I knew Sinisa Glogovac as a colleague of mine. As for this other person, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long had you worked with Mr. Glogovac, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Glogovac was in the service while I was in the service, but he was in Zvornik; I was in Sokolac. Perhaps we would meet two or three times about some meetings, things like that. But we did not have any direct contacts in the form of exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard a good amount of testimony that there were portions of that column numbering in the hundreds that were feared to be heading towards the Zepa area and in some cases in fact made it to the Zepa area. When do you recall receiving that information, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I received this information from Mr. Avdo Palic in the course of his interview, and he told me that a certain number of soldiers of the 28th Division had crossed into the territory of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so it's clear for the record, sir, what you are telling the Trial Chamber is that it was not until your interviews with Avdo Palic in late July 1995 that you ever heard about any threat to the Zepa area, any movement into the Zepa area by men who were fleeing the Srebrenica enclave following the fall of that enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you interviewed Colonel Palic, sir, did you interview him alone on those two occasions, or were you accompanied by anyone from your agency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a colleague of mine. We always did interviews in pairs. That was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your colleague's name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Cajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And prior to your interviews with Colonel Palic, did you attempt to learn whether or not the VRS had interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no need for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Wouldn't you have found it helpful to learn from the VRS information that they would have obtained from their interviews with Colonel Palic prior to you sitting down with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the time, were you aware whether or not the VRS had interviewed Colonel Palic either before your first interview and between your second interview or after your final interview? Did you ever come into that information on or about this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not get this information, but it was logical to assume that the colleagues from the military security had interviewed him about those things that they were interested in, that they needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The notes that you told us about that you and your colleague took of your interview with Colonel Palic, where are those?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: After every interview that we did with any person regardless of their status, whether those were prisoners of war or refugees, Bosnians, Croats, Muslims, an official record was made of this interview, and it was sent to the centre of our service. As far as I know, those documents are no longer in the service because it was handed over to the representatives of the international community in Bosnia and Herzegovina because they seized a total -- all of them sometime in the year 2000. So as far as I know, these documents are no longer in possession of the service but are in possession of the international community and its bodies that are charged with keeping peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they should have those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the notes that you described went out under your name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The notes indicate who gave the statement, who took the statement, and who was present when the statement was given. There was the heading on each note indicating the organ that took the statement, the person who actually took the statement, and also the person who gave the statement. The person who gave the statement had to sign the statement at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3523, please. Take a moment, sir, and review the document that appears on the right. Let us know when you are ready to have the page turned.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of the B/C/S document, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I've never seen it before, but I see that this was issued by the State Security Service and that the signatory is the head of the service Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to the first page of the document at B/C/S, sir. If we could scroll down on the B/C/S to the last paragraph, please. We see here that it says, "After the Muslim side from Zepa rejected to hand over the conscripts, the commander of the Muslim Brigade from that area was 'detained,' and the RDB workers had been interviewing him." Now, this is a document dated 28 July 1995. The RDB workers to whom this report is referring are yourself and the colleague you identified a few moments ago; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. Probably it was the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you have any information that any other RDB workers interviewed Colonel Palic other than yourself and your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any explanation for why the word "detained" is in quotation marks, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any explanation whatsoever why it is in quotation marks. I suppose that the meaning is it was meant that he was detained, within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we continue on in this paragraph, it indicates that "The information we have obtained to date includes the strength, weapons, plans, and movements of Muslim soldiers from Zepa. Palic claims that there are about 2.000 military-age men in that area, 400 to 500 of whom have arrived from Srebrenica. Half of them are armed mainly with infantry weapons, and the rest are unarmed." And then the paragraph goes on and discusses the planned breakthrough. Sir, there's nothing in this report talking about an investigation into war crimes committed by the Zepa forces, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There's nothing there about that. This report was drafted by the top of the service; i.e., our information contained in our report is what I told you about all the acts that had been committed and that we learned about. However, at the moment when this report was being sent to the minister, the priority was to highlight the remainder of the troops and the withdrawal and passing through our territory. As for the information that we obtained about the crimes and who committed them, that would be used subsequently when criminal reports were to be filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, this information that's contained in this report is coming from no one else but yourself and your colleague; you just stated that no other RDB workers interviewed Colonel Palic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this refers only to this passage where it says the Muslim side in Zepa, but there are other passages here, as well, that speak about the events in the territory of Srebrenica which points to the fact that all the daily reports that arrived from the territory either from Sokolac, Zvornik, or other parts are then incorporated into a combined report that is drafted in the evening and forwarded to the superior authorities. So the only part that is related to what I had fed into the report is in this passage. The rest probably came from the other colleagues and what they have provided as an input for the collective report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just focusing on this one little passage here, but we see that the information that it's referring to includes the strength, weapons, plans, movements of the Muslim soldiers from Zepa and then goes on to describe in more detail some of the military information that you told us a few moments ago you had no interest in. How do you explain that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It is very easy to explain, and this is the explanation: The information contained in this passage here were taken out from the context of the entire report that had been forwarded; and in that statement, most of the statement concerns the crimes and the perpetrators thereof. However, the only thing that was forwarded from my report into the combined report for that day was the part that you are reading in those documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's because that was vital information for the State Security Service to know at that time, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's why you asked Colonel Palic all kinds of questions about military matters like those contained in this passage, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Like I've told you already, we asked him various questions in order to obtain information about the possible infiltration of their groups that could have threatened the security of the villages and the population in the territory of Republika Srpska that were along the access of their possible withdrawal in the future. That's why these issues were of some relevance for the security of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So please tell the Trial Chamber what efforts you undertook to obtain information from the VRS, from the security and intelligence administration, or any other element within the VRS to keep your superiors as informed as possible about the security threats that were facing your area during this time that you were interviewing Colonel Palic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment I did not rely on anybody, nor did I obtain any information save for the information that I myself had obtained through my own investigative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So you never called Pecanac, Carkic, or Colonel Beara or anybody; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This is my testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can we have 2D528 on the e-court, please. While we are waiting for that document, sir, when you last saw Colonel Palic, in whose custody and control was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: All that time, Mr. Palic was in the custody and control of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you no doubt are aware that Colonel Palic's whereabouts remain unknown to the public to this day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not to this day. Around the year 2000, I learned from the TV that a commission had been set up to search the missing persons and that one of its tasks or its only task was to locate for the missing colonel of the BH Army, Avdo Palic. Actually, it was only then that I learned that he had been missing and that he was still missing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please share with the Trial Chamber any information, sir, that you might have from any source, as a state security officer, through your contacts with the VRS, any information that you might have as to where Colonel Palic is or where his remains might be found. Please share that information, if you have any, with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information at all. I don't know anything about his further movements, about his further destiny from the moment when I did my interview with him onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at this first page of 2D528, please. Do you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down a little bit, if you look at number 9, we see an individual named Ramiz Ridzal, son of Sacire, born in 1951. The individuals on this list, sir, you interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw any of them except for Avdo Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you, sir, that Mr. Ridzal remains on the missing list compiled by the ICMP [sic]. If we turn to page 5 -- of the ICRC. And if we see number 82, sir, on page 5 of the B/C/S of the original, Mr. Amir Imamovic, son of Mehmed. Were you aware, sir, that his remains were found in a mass grave in the Rogatica area in the village of - I'll try to pronounce it - Vragalovi. Do you know that location, sir, Vragalovi?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we have got 5 minutes left. If you could try and finish within those five minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we have a DNA-matched identification of the remains of this individual who is on this list who was last seen at that prison in Rogatica in the company of Mr. Torlak, whom you interviewed, as a prisoner. Do you have any information as to why these two individuals, in the case of the former, are missing, and in the case of the latter, was found in a mass grave in Rogatica? Do you have any information you can share with us on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I have no information whatsoever about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are aware that the column that withdrew from Srebrenica consisted of both soldiers and civilians, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there were soldiers of the 28th Division exclusively, and I'm not aware of the fact that civilians might have been in the same column as the soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To this day you've never heard that information, sir; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't understand the context of your question, sir. Would you please be so kind and give me a specific question, a concrete question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that to this day you never received any information that that column of withdrawing men and boys from Srebrenica contained civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that because I watched TV clips where I saw men wearing civilian clothes, but whether they were truly civilians or still members of the 28th Division I believe remains a topic of further analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you would certainly allow, would you not, for the possibility that there were numbers of civilians among those thousands of men and boys, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I will allow for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a possibility that there might have been some civilians, but their number was negligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is a question for speculation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move and conclude, I think, at this point. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that there were as many as 7 or 800, perhaps more, men from Zepa who made it to Serbia primarily by swimming, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What did you say in terms of the numbers of men from Zepa that made it over to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I had at that time, the figure would be anything between 800 and 900 soldiers, members of the 285th Brigade, and I emphasize: They were soldiers. They made a decision to cross over the Drina and go to Serbia. Now, how they crossed and who they surrendered to over there, I don't know. Later on, I learned that the figure was around 800 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you didn't interview 800 prisoners from Zepa, did you, that made it to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not talk to a single one of them who had crossed over to Serbia, nor did I myself ever cross over to Serbia in order to collect any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So you really have no firm basis based on interviews either conducted by yourself or statements taken from those individuals to conclude that there were no civilians among the men that made it over to Serbia from Zepa, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, there were no civilians who made it over from Zepa to Serbia, according to what I know, and that would be my final answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you allow for the possibility as there was in Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. That is speculation now, so let's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one brief question for clarification more than anything else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, in answering my learned friend's questions about the reasons why Avdo Palic was detained, you said that he had refused to disarm around 1.500 men in the Zepa brigade. I want a precise answer from you. Did this concern the disarmament of the complete enclave of Zepa or just one part of one military unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN VOJINOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I remember, based on the information that we had at the time, one of the items in the agreement on the disarmament of the 285th Brigade in Zepa was for the soldiers of that brigade with all of their weapons to go to the UNPROFOR base in Zepa, surrender their weapons, and the Red Cross should have mediated in the exchange of these soldiers for the soldiers of the Republika Srpska army who were detained by the BiH army. Since this item of the agreement had not been complied with, Avdo Palic was detained and kept in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no questions from the Bench, which means, Mr. Vojinovic, that your testimony ends here. Thank you for coming over to testify. Before you leave the courtroom, on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I wish you successful work and stay here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stand adjourned now until tomorrow morning at 9 o'clock. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
